note: A ratio, not a count. Absolute survivor counts rise with every
line added -- new code means new mutants, so a healthy change
with good tests would trip an absolute ratchet. The score below
is killed / (killed + survived): it stays comparable as the
codebase grows and only moves when tests get better or worse.
Not every survivor is a gap. About a quarter only change a log
or error message, which nothing asserts on by design. Others are
equivalent: `if not mismatched` decides when the read-back loop
exits, not what it returns, so killing it would mean asserting on
timing -- a worse test than the mutant is a risk.
Mutants with no covering test are excluded from the score rather
than counted as failures: the tests that drive a module through a
real subprocess load the original source, so a mutation run says
nothing about what they cover. See
docs/decisions/0005-mutation-testing-scope.md.
0.65 -> 0.67 (2026-08-19), and this is the largest rise so far,
against the largest growth so far: 2726 -> 3745 mutants, over a
0.678 -> 0.689 (2026-08-20) by reading the survivors instead of
accepting the number. Five tests, 42 mutants killed, and three of
the five were real defects rather than test gaps:
- `device = None` inside reconcile_now survived everything. With
no register model every policy falls back to REMEMBER, so
pinning stops working entirely -- and the tests that covered
the pinned branch all used a `[pin]` override, which is read
*before* the model and so kept working.
- `fresh = config` -> `fresh = None`: nothing exercised SIGHUP on
a machine with no routing.conf, where the running config is all
there is. That path ended in reconcile_now(None, ...).
- Nothing checked that a reload keeps the ports the backend is
bound to. Taking new ports from the file would write to a port
nobody is on, silently, because OSC over UDP does not report
delivery.
The rest of the ~100 survivors in that code were log text and
arguments to log calls -- the quarter this file has always said is
not a gap. What made the difference was that reading them also
exposed a design fact: in reconcile_now only `kept` decides what is
written, and `problems` was computed purely to be logged. The log
line said '%d to correct', which reads as though only those were
written. It now says what it does.
Measured on a cleared cache, as CI does, in 56 minutes.

measured.cache: cleared before the run, as CI does

why_it_moved: 0.690 -> 0.678 with the reconcile triggers. New code that is
signal, subprocess and socket plumbing rather than pure
functions, which is the shape the note above says kills fewer
mutants. The fall confirmed the rule rather than contradicting
it -- and it was worth reading rather than accepting, because
five of the survivors turned out to be real gaps.

note: Measured independently on a GitHub runner. Five mutants differ,
which is the timing-sensitive tail: the suite binds real UDP
sockets and drives threads. not_covered agrees exactly, and that
is the number a re-baseline turns on.

floor_note: The gate is min_score - tolerance = 0.64. That is the number that
matters: the score may not fall below it. min_score itself is set
at the measured 0.655 rounded down, so the policy neither fails
nor nags on the run it was recorded from -- a baseline that prints
'raise me' on every CI run teaches people to ignore it.
